name: Hana Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day in your life now, and what your working life was like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts with the market at eight, because the vegetables are better early. Then I do a bit of sewing, mending coats and hemming trousers for neighbours for a few coins, and I pick up my grandson Tomas from school at three. My husband Pavel, who drove a city bus for thirty-five years, sits with the crossword. I worked as a machine sewer at the Karlin garment factory for thirty-six years, until it shut and I left at sixty-two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did that factory teach you, and what's different about your days now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The factory made work jackets and uniforms. It was noisy, and we were paid by the piece, so your hands never stopped. We lost jobs when the orders went abroad, so I've seen what it's like when work disappears. We live in a small flat in a block with high maintenance fees. Our two pensions cover it, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's what I thought. Everyone gets excited and then nothing much happens. At the market, my neighbour would say it's a toy for the rich, and I'd agree partly. I'd say I'd believe it when I see it help someone get their pension on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not a lot. The tablet my daughter Eva set up for me helps me with recipes and translating the odd letter, and sometimes I ask the assistant for how to mend a zip. It's useful, but it doesn't change my life. My worry is money: the flat's fees went up 8 percent this year and our pensions didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the mending, about six jobs a week, which brings in 60 or so. I'd go on using the tablet as I do. I'd keep taking Tomas to school, which saves Eva the childcare cost. And I'd keep an eye on the fees, ask at the residents' meeting if they can be held down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels all right, I'm used to waiting for storms and nothing happening. But there's always a worry that the next fee rise will be the one that tips us. I'd say I'm a bit tense, a bit tired, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the fees went up and your pensions didn't. Which bill would you look at first if it rose again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If fees went up more, I'd have to cut the mending supplies, which is silly because that's what brings in money. More likely I'd stop the weekly cake with Tomas and the bus ticket to see my sister. Pavel would say go ahead, and then quietly give up his coffee at the club. We're like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You help your neighbour Marta. What sort of things does she need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If routine tasks go to AI, good, let them have the boring parts. I wish the paper forms for pensions were easier. I'd say the tablet helps, but my friend Marta (a neighbour of mine) can't use one and her kids are far away. She struggles, and I help her.

say: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it help someone get their **pension** on time.
I'd say let the machines have the **boring parts**.
think: The tablet is useful but my real worry is **money**, with fees up 8 percent and pensions flat.
I'm used to waiting for **storms** that don't come.
do: Keep **mending** about six jobs a week, which brings in around 60.
Keep taking my grandson **Tomas** to school to save my daughter childcare costs.
Ask at the residents' meeting if the **fees** can be held down.
feel: I feel a bit **tense** and tired, not scared.
S0.quote: The flat's fees went up 8 percent this year and our pensions didn't.
fieldNote: Her worry is **building fees** and the pension, not AI.
Steady and practical, she uses the tablet when it helps.
Helps her neighbour Marta, who can't use a tablet.

steps.text: Keep mending coats and trousers for six neighbours a week
Take Tomas to school daily to save Eva childcare costs
Ask the residents' meeting to hold the maintenance fees down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd say to Eva, who works at a call centre for an insurance firm: prepare. They've already started using a chatbot for the easy calls, and half her team has been moved to the hard ones. I'd say it at the dinner table and I'd say the firm should tell its workers the plan, not leave them guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly through Eva. She earns about 1,900 and pays the biggest share of her own mortgage. If the firm cuts her team, she'd lose it and we'd be the ones to help, which we can't properly. I'd worry about Tomas too, because his mother's income pays his football and his school trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Eva and ask her plainly what she'd do. I'd go with her to look at evening courses, maybe bookkeeping or something in health admin. I'd offer to take Tomas four days a week so she can study. And I'd ask the neighbours who have kids in different jobs what they'd advise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing at a bus stop watching a bus that isn't yours go by, but you know your daughter's on it. I'm not afraid for myself but I'm afraid for her. It's a mother's fear, and it isn't polite to say at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Eva on the evening she told you her team was being cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If she was laid off, I'd give her about 100 a month from the mending, which is all I can. Pavel would cut his club coffees and we'd drop the cable. We'd maybe even ask my brother in the country whether she and Tomas could stay with him for a few months if the mortgage went badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned maybe bookkeeping or health admin. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd tell her is don't pretend it's fine. I'd say, ask for training at the firm, and use the tools before they use you. I've learned a bit on the tablet and it's not so hard. A machine that checks claims might not know what the old woman on the phone really means.

say: I'd say the firm should tell its workers the **plan**, not leave them guessing.
I'd tell my daughter to ask for **training** at the firm and use the tools before they use you.
think: The danger is through **Eva**, who earns about 1,900 and carries most of her mortgage.
If her team is cut, we'd have to help and we **can't** properly.
do: Sit down with Eva and look at **evening courses** in bookkeeping or health admin.
Offer to take Tomas **four days** a week so she can study.
Ask neighbours with kids in other jobs for **advice**.
feel: It feels like watching a **bus** go by that isn't mine but my daughter is on it.
S1.quote: A machine that checks claims might not know what the old woman on the phone really means.
fieldNote: Her fear passes through her **daughter's** call centre job, not her own.
Offers childcare as her practical help, since money is not hers to give.

steps.text: Offer to mind Tomas four days a week so Eva can study

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, goodness. Two years is no time to find a new job, never mind a new life. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. And I'd say the government must prepare right away, not hold meetings. I'd go to the residents' meeting and say we need to look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm very worried, because it'd be Eva's job first, and maybe the whole call centre. The mortgage on her place is 920 a month, and if she lost her wage, we'd have to find that or she'd sell. Pavel and I have no savings to help. I'd think about the factory closing all over again. The factory closing was slow, this would be quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Eva and Tomas to come and live with us if things went wrong, though our flat is tiny. I'd get Pavel to ask at the bus depot if his old friends have any ideas. I'd ask the council and the church group about help. I'd put every spare coin into a jar, and I'd sew as much as I can, even if the pay is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a cold stone in the stomach. I'd wake at four every morning. I'd cook for everyone and say it's fine, because that's how I show I'm coping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does two years feel so much worse than five, in your daughter's case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on stuff comes three years later, which matters a little for me, because sewing is still done by people and the robots are far from fine fabric. But it's not my job that counts here, it's my daughter's. With two years she has no time to change course, and I'd say that makes it the worst for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about Pavel's pension payments in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also worry about Pavel. He's sixty-eight and has a bad heart, so if the pension office goes wrong, if the payments get delayed, we'd be stuck. I'd go to the office and ask for a written promise, I know it's silly, but I'd feel better.

say: I'd say two years is no time to find a **new job**, never mind a new life.
I'd tell the residents' meeting we must **look out** for each other.
think: It would be **Eva's** job first and maybe the whole call centre.
Her mortgage is **920** a month, and we have no savings to help.
do: Ask Eva and **Tomas** to live with us if things go wrong.
Ask the council and church group about **help** and put spare coins in a jar.

feel: It feels like a **cold stone** in my stomach and I'd wake at four.
S2.quote: The factory closing was slow, this would be quick.
fieldNote: The **two-year clock** makes her relive the factory closure, quicker this time.
Cooks for everyone to show she is coping.

steps.text: Offer our flat to Eva and Tomas if the mortgage fails
Ask the council and church group about help for pensioners
Take every mending job I can find

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more like it. I'd say get ready. I'd tell Eva and the younger ones at the market that this is the moment to get a skill, and I'd tell the council that older people need classes too. I'd say it plainly, no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still worrying but I can see a road. In five years Eva could have a new qualification and Tomas would be older and need less minding. I'd be sixty-nine. The big question is whether the pension and prices hold. I think if it comes slowly, it might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Eva sign up for an evening course this winter. I'd save 25 a month from the mending money in a separate envelope. I'd ask Marta and the other neighbours to form a group where we share what we know about the tablet and the forms. And I'd keep an eye on how the pension changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like cold weather coming. You get your coat and wood ready. I'm anxious but I'm not scared stiff, because there's something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the neighbours' tablet group do at its first meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What five years changes is that my daughter Eva can change jobs before she's pushed out, not after. That's a very different feeling. I'd say if she moves into health admin or teaching support, she could be fine. And I'd teach Tomas to sew a button, so he's got something practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you and Pavel to move into Eva's building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also think about whether Pavel and I should move to a cheaper place, maybe into Eva's building if there's a vacancy. That would cut fees. But it would also be hard leaving the neighbours. I'd think about it, and talk about it with my sister.

say: I'd tell younger people this is the moment to get a **skill** and tell the council older people need classes too.
I'd say it plainly, with **no drama**.
think: I can see a **road**: Eva could retrain and Tomas would need less minding.
The big question is whether the **pension** and prices hold.
do: Help Eva sign up for an **evening course** this winter.
Save **25 a month** from the mending in a separate envelope.
Start a **tablet group** with Marta and the neighbours.
feel: It feels like **cold weather** coming: you get your coat and wood ready.
S3.quote: What five years changes is that my daughter Eva can change jobs before she's pushed out, not after.
fieldNote: More time turns fear into a **plan** for her daughter's retraining.
Considers moving to a cheaper home near family.
Builds neighbourhood help through the tablet group.

steps.text: Help Eva enrol in an evening course this winter
Save 25 a month from mending in a separate envelope
Start a neighbours' tablet group with Marta
Look at moving into Eva's building to cut fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say, that's a generation. I'd tell Eva and Tomas to take their time but not waste it. I'd say we should keep the pension office running with real people. I'd tell the council to start training classes for older folks now, because we're the ones who learn slowly and need the most time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel better. I'd be seventy-four, and Pavel seventy-eight, if he's still here. A lot of this will happen when we're old or gone. But I'd be worried for Tomas. It's his world. I'd want him to learn something solid, with his hands and his head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sewing and mending, and save 15 a month. I'd help Eva retrain at her own pace, and I'd show Tomas how to sew and cook, because those are lasting skills. I'd keep up with the tablet and ask Eva or Tomas to teach me the new things. And I'd ask Pavel to see the doctor regularly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels far away, like looking at a mountain from the train. I'm not scared. I'm curious, and a bit sad about what Tomas will have to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is the longest warning. What do you do with the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd probably get more comfortable with the tools. I don't love them, but I've learned that when you've got time, you can learn anything. Two years is too short for that, and five is okay. Ten is like learning a language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want Tomas to hold on to from your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas that when he grows up, some of the best jobs will be the ones where you look after people, because people still want a real face. I'd say it over a cup of hot chocolate, with his feet on the kitchen chair, which I'd tell him off for.

say: I'd tell Eva and Tomas to take their time but not **waste it**.
I'd tell the council to start **classes** for older folks now.
think: I'd feel **better**, since a lot of this would happen when we're old or gone.
My worry is **Tomas**, because it's his world.
do: Teach Tomas to **sew and cook**, which are lasting skills.
Ask Eva or Tomas to teach me the new things on the **tablet**.
feel: It feels far away, like a **mountain** from the train, and a little sad for Tomas.
S4.quote: Some of the best jobs will be the ones where you look after people, because people still want a real face.
fieldNote: With ten years she is **calmer** and thinks of grandchildren.
Wants lasting hands-on skills for Tomas, her **grandson**, more than any credential.
Learned that time makes learning possible.

steps.text: Keep mending for neighbours and save 15 a month
Put 15 a month into the post office account
Teach Tomas to sew and cook at weekends
Ask Eva and Tomas to teach me new tablet tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Eva's job and the mortgage. What would help is a decent income guarantee for people who lose work, retraining paid for by the firms, and the fees in my building being held down. And the pension office keeping real people on the phone, for Marta and me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the factory taught me you can lose a life's work in a month. People think old folks don't know what's coming, but we've seen it. We know what it feels like when the work goes. We just don't make a fuss.

headlineQuote: People think old folks don't know what's coming, but we've seen it. We know what it feels like when the work goes.
portrait: Hana is **64**, a retired factory sewer who mends clothes for neighbours and minds her grandson.
She uses a tablet now and then, and is **practical** more than afraid of the technology.
Her fears run through her daughter **Eva's** call centre job and the pension and fees.
She moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as the warning shrinks.
biggestWorry: Two years worries her most, because of **Eva's** job and mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: An **income guarantee**, firm-paid retraining and held-down building fees.
